summary: Describes an SMTP service extension, REQUIRETLS, and a message header, TLS-Required, that let a sender ask that a message travel only over properly secured TLS connections. Normal STARTTLS is opportunistic, so delivery is favored over security unless this is used.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally email may travel in an open envelope if the secure path is blocked. This lets the sender say to deliver only via the sealed route.

questions: what does the tls-required header do
how to force tls for email delivery
subtitle: Lets an email sender demand encrypted, authenticated delivery, or explicitly waive it, one message at a time.

tldr.problem: SMTP encryption with STARTTLS is opportunistic: if TLS cannot be negotiated, the message is sent without transport encryption, and clients often accept invalid certificates.
tldr.mechanism: A REQUIRETLS parameter on the MAIL FROM command makes the sender refuse delivery unless a verified TLS session to a REQUIRETLS-capable server is possible. A TLS-Required: No header field does the opposite and asks that recipient TLS policy be ignored.
tldr.outcome: Senders choose per message whether security or delivery comes first. If the requirements cannot be met, the message is not sent and a non-delivery notification goes back.

today: RFC 8689 is a Proposed Standard (Standards Track, November 2019). The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Opportunistic TLS Falls Short
sections.content:
The RFC 3207 STARTTLS extension lets an SMTP client and server set up a TLS-protected session. By default it is used only if both sides agree. If negotiation fails, the message goes out without transport encryption. It is also common for a client to negotiate TLS even when the server's certificate is invalid.

Policy mechanisms such as DANE and MTA-STS can require TLS for some domains, but they do not let the sender mark which messages are sensitive and which should be relayed even if TLS fails. The RFC lists the attacks this enables: passive eavesdropping on connections without TLS, interfering with the protocol so TLS is never negotiated, and a man-in-the-middle exploiting the lack of server authentication.

REQUIRETLS has two parts. An SMTP service extension says a message MUST travel over a TLS session with specified security properties. A message header field, TLS-Required, asks that recipient-side policy be ignored, and it can pass through MTAs that do not support REQUIRETLS.
sections.plainLanguage: Email usually tries to lock the door when it travels, but if the lock is jammed it just walks through anyway. This is a way for the sender to say 'do not go through unless the door locks'.

sections.title: The Extension and the Header Field
sections.content:
The extension's EHLO keyword is REQUIRETLS. It adds one optional parameter, also called REQUIRETLS, to the MAIL FROM command. The parameter has no value, and it raises the maximum MAIL FROM line length by 11 octets. No new SMTP verbs are defined. The extension is valid for message relay, submission and LMTP.

The TLS-Required header field has one REQUIRED parameter, No. With it, the SMTP client SHOULD try to send the message even if it cannot negotiate STARTTLS, ignoring recipient policy such as MTA-STS and DANE, but SHOULD still negotiate STARTTLS if it is available. At most one instance may appear in a message. The RFC suggests a use: reporting a misconfigured mail server, such as one with an expired certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two notes a sender can attach. One is stamped on the envelope: 'secure delivery only'. The other is written inside: 'if the secure way is broken, send it anyway'.

sections.title: When REQUIRETLS May Be Used
sections.content:
The REQUIRETLS option MUST only be given in an SMTP session that meets all of these conditions:

  • The session itself MUST use TLS.
  • If the server was found through an MX lookup, its name MUST be validated by a DNSSEC signature on the MX record, or by an MTA-STS policy.
  • The server's certificate MUST verify through a trust chain the client trusts, or through DANE.
  • After STARTTLS, the server MUST advertise REQUIRETLS in its next EHLO response.

The last rule means a server that advertises REQUIRETLS is promising to honour the requirement and to enforce it for onward transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the sender uses the 'secure only' stamp, it checks the road is really secure: the mail server is who it claims to be, the lock works, and the server promises to keep the rule going.

sections.title: How Senders and Receivers Behave
sections.content:
A server that receives the REQUIRETLS option MUST tag the message as needing REQUIRETLS handling. A message with only the TLS-Required header is tagged with that header's option. If the MAIL FROM parameter is present, the header is ignored.

When sending a message that requires TLS, the client MTA looks up the server, validates the MX name with MTA-STS if there is no valid DNSSEC signature, opens an EHLO session, establishes TLS and authenticates the certificate, and checks that REQUIRETLS is advertised after TLS. If any step fails it sends QUIT and tries the next MX host. If none works it MUST NOT send the message and MUST send a non-delivery notification. The status codes it SHOULD use are 5.7.30 (REQUIRETLS support required) and 5.7.10 (Encryption needed).

For TLS-Required: No messages, the client attempts STARTTLS and follows recipient policy but does not fail if that is unsuccessful. If a server itself insists on STARTTLS, a non-delivery notification MUST be returned. A mail user agent making the first submission MUST either use REQUIRETLS or include the header; how it decides is left to the implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender with a 'secure only' letter tries each post office in turn. If none has a safe, locked route, it does not send the letter and tells the writer so.

sections.title: Bounces and Reorigination
sections.content:
Bounce messages carry important details, such as the original header, so they MUST be protected like the original and MUST also use the REQUIRETLS option. A bounce is sent with an empty return-path, and the parameter SHOULD NOT cause it to be discarded if the next hop lacks REQUIRETLS. The server MUST act as if RET=HDRS were present, and RET=FULL is disregarded. Senders should be able to receive mail over REQUIRETLS too, or bounces may be lost.

Mediators such as mailing lists, Sieve filters and vacation responders that create new messages should apply the incoming REQUIRETLS requirement to the new messages to the extent feasible. Redistributing a TLS-required message to many addresses could mean some recipients do not get it.
sections.plainLanguage: If a secure letter cannot be delivered, the note saying so must travel just as securely. And anyone who re-sends a secure letter should keep it secure.

sections.title: What REQUIRETLS Defends Against
sections.content:
These points apply to the service extension, not to the header field. REQUIRETLS is generally effective against passive eavesdroppers. Against active attacks it detects a damaged STARTTLS command (for example one changed to XXXXXXXX) and declines to send in the clear. It requires successful certificate validation, which stops a man-in-the-middle terminating TLS. It also requires MX validation by DNSSEC or MTA-STS, which counters spoofed MX records.

This is transport-layer protection only. Messages are not encrypted end to end and are visible to the MTAs on the path. A bad-actor MTA could strip tags or misstate support, but such MTAs are outside the threat model. Content that MTAs should not see MUST use end-to-end encryption such as OpenPGP or S/MIME.

The TLS-Required: No header can conflict with a recipient's DANE or MTA-STS policy. It tells the client MTA to behave as if it did not support them. The recipient domain can still require TLS by refusing messages when STARTTLS was not negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: The sealed route stops snoopers on the road, but every post office on the way can still open the letter. For real secrets, write in a code only the reader can unlock.
